name: Mesha
source_summary: King of Moab who rebelled against Israel by withholding tribute after Ahab's death; when a coalition of Israel, Judah, and Edom invaded Moab and besieged him at Kir-hareseth, he broke through Edom's lines in a failed attempt to escape, then, in desperation, sacrificed his own firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall.
family_friendly_summary: Mesha was the king of Moab, a nation east of Israel that raised sheep. Moab had been paying tribute -- large numbers of lambs and wool -- to the king of Israel, but after King Ahab died, Mesha refused to keep paying. In response, the kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom joined together and marched against Moab. God helped the allied armies through the prophet Elisha, and they pushed Mesha back to his last stronghold, the city of Kir-hareseth. Cornered and desperate, Mesha tried to break through the enemy lines but failed. Scripture records that he then did something very dark and tragic: he sacrificed his own oldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. This terrible act shows how far people can fall when they turn to false, cruel gods instead of trusting the true God.
adult_story: Mesha, king of Moab, is introduced in 2 Kings 3 as a sheep breeder who had paid Israel a heavy annual tribute of lambs and wool, but who 'rebelled against the king of Israel' after Ahab's death (3:4-5). King Jehoram of Israel responded by allying with Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom to invade Moab. After their armies nearly perished from lack of water in the wilderness, the prophet Elisha intervened, promising both water and victory (3:9-19). The coalition routed Moab's forces and besieged Mesha's remaining stronghold at Kir-hareseth (3:24-25). Cornered, Mesha attempted a desperate breakout with seven hundred swordsmen to reach the king of Edom, but failed (3:26). In his final desperation, he took 'his oldest son who was to reign in his place, and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall' (3:27) -- a shocking act of child sacrifice to his god Chemosh, offered in the sight of the besieging armies. Scripture records that 'there came great wrath against Israel, and they departed from him and returned to their own land' (3:27), a verse whose meaning is debated among interpreters but which at minimum marks the campaign's abrupt, unsettling end. Mesha's story is preserved in Scripture without any softening of its horror, a stark picture of pagan desperation contrasted with the true God who explicitly forbids child sacrifice (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31).
